newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Nestle's 96 sales up, sees solid 97.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Nestle's 96 sales up, sees solid 97.

text.p: Nestle SA forecast rising sales and profits for 1997 and reported on Tuesday that 1996 turnover grew 7.1 percent to a record 60.5 billion Swiss francs ($42.78 billion), boosted by volume gains and a weakening Swiss franc.
The world's biggest food company, vowing to end problems in its U.S. beverage business that weighed on 1996 turnover, said it expected sales volume would keep growing in 1997.
"Barring adverse currency developments, the group should therefore register another increase in sales and profit," it said in a statement from company headquarters in Vevey.

Nestle, which in addition to its famed chocolate and coffee controls diverse top brands ranging from Perrier and Vittel mineral waters to Chambourcy yoghurts, the Ortega mexican food range and Friskies pet foods, gave no profit figures for 1996. But it said net profit growth should outstrip the rate at which sales increased.

"I think generally we take a very constructive outlook for 1997. We feel that Europe has a lot of momentum, especially eastern Europe where we did very well last year," finance director Mario Corti told Reuters Financial Television.
"We have solid positions in virtually all the emerging markets in the world and we believe the problems in North America will be corrected as well."

He was referring to "trade loading", in which companies rush out product at the end of the year to inflate sales, a Nestle spokesman said. The problem, which Nestle has already addressed, hit sales of instant coffee hard in a key market.
Corti said U.S. results would improve. "It is hard to say just how much we will be able to pick up, but we will definitely have put the problems we encounted last year behind us."
He said Nestle stood to gain handsomely in 1997 if the dollar remains strong against the Swiss franc.

"At the current rate this will have quite an impact on sales converted into Swiss francs," he said. "We have to bear in mind the dollar is trading at around 1.41 (francs) right now, whereas the weighted rate...for 1996 is 1.24. That's quite a difference, but we will have to see how things develop over the year."

For the first time since 1993, exchange rates had a positive effect on 1996 sales, accounting for 1.4 percentage points of growth, Nestle said. Sales volume growth, excluding acquistions and disinvestments, was 2.7 percent.
The Asia/Pacific region, Africa and the Middle East posted strong volume growth. Growth was above average in Europe, due primarily to rapid expansion in central and eastern Europe.

"In the Americas, Latin America achieved above-average growth, whereas the U.S. market's overall growth did not live up to expectations, particularly due to transitional problems in the beverage division," it said.
Nestle shares advanced on the headline sales figure, which was at the higher end of expectations, before droppping back to hover near Monday's close at 1,469 francs.
Analysts gave mostly favourable reviews, but some said Nestle should have done even better given the weakening franc.
"This is pretty positive," said Anne Alexandre at Credit Suisse First Boston in London. "This is at the top range of the consensus, just below the 60.6 billion I was expecting."

But Wilhelm Blaeuer at Pictet et Cie in Geneva said Nestle should have been able to exploit the currency factor to wring more sales from abroad. He said 2.7 percent volume growth was also below his forecast, and played down Nestle's rosy outlook.
"Are they saying something which might induce anybody to upgrade their estimates? I don't think so," Blaeuer said.
"I simply don't see where the huge potential is for next year and the year after," he added.
